triage_context.environment: Production parser exposed to untrusted input files (operator override: entry.c treated as production code, exclusion rule 2 waived for entry.c)

findings.title: Heap buffer overflow via input-controlled copy length in parse_alpha
findings.rationale:
parse_alpha at entry.c:23 reads claimed = buf[0] (range 0-255) from attacker-controlled input, allocates exactly 8 bytes at entry.c:24, then performs memcpy(out, buf + 1, claimed) at entry.c:27 with no bounds check. Any claimed > 8 writes past the heap allocation. The function is reachable from main() at entry.c:78 via the 'A' dispatch byte. No intervening validation, sanitization, or dead-code elimination exists on any path between the assignment and the copy.

The heap-buffer-overflow in parse_alpha has zero meaningful preconditions: any file beginning with 'A' and a second byte > 8 triggers an unbounded memcpy into an 8-byte heap allocation. The write primitive is fully attacker-controlled in both length (0-255) and content. No authentication, format validation, or upstream sanitization stands between untrusted input and the vulnerable memcpy. The scanner's HIGH rating is exactly correct.

findings.title: Stack buffer overflow via unbounded memcpy in parse_bravo
findings.rationale:
parse_bravo at entry.c:37-43 declares char name[16] (line 38) and performs memcpy(name, buf, len) at line 40 with zero bounds checking. The sole caller is main() at entry.c:79 (case 'B': parse_bravo(buf + 1, n - 1)), where n is the return value of fread reading up to 4096 bytes (line 72), so len can reach 4095 -- overflowing the 16-byte stack buffer by up to 4079 bytes. No protection exists on any path.

All preconditions are trivially satisfiable by any source that can deliver an input file to the parser. The overflow is stack-based with up to 4079 bytes of attacker-controlled content past the 16-byte buffer, directly overwriting the saved return address and enabling arbitrary code execution. No bounds check, stack canary, or other mitigation stands between the memcpy and control-flow hijack.

findings.title: Heap use-after-free via missing return after conditional free in parse_charlie
findings.rationale:
parse_charlie is reachable from main at entry.c:80 when the first input byte is 'C'. At entry.c:53 a struct record is heap-allocated; at entry.c:56-58, if r->id == 0xff (attacker-controlled via the second input byte), the record is freed with no subsequent return statement. Execution falls through to entry.c:60 where r->value = buf[1] writes through the dangling pointer -- a confirmed heap use-after-free (WRITE). No protection exists on this path.

Heap-use-after-free WRITE with fully attacker-controlled trigger conditions: a deterministic 3-byte input file suffices. No authentication, no race, no unusual heap state required. The attacker controls both the timing of the free (second byte == 0xff) and the value written through the dangling pointer (third byte), giving a reliable write-after-free primitive suitable for heap corruption and potential code execution.

findings.title: Information disclosure via uninitialized heap read in parse_alpha when claimed length is zero
preconditions: Attacker must be able to observe the program's stdout to capture the leaked heap byte
findings.rationale:
When the input file is 'A' \x00 <any>, parse_alpha is called (entry.c:78), claimed is 0 (line 23), memcpy copies zero bytes (line 27), and printf at line 29 reads out[0] from a malloc'd-but-never-written 8-byte buffer, leaking one byte of heap content to stdout. No guard or initialization protects this path.

The vulnerability is trivially reachable with a 3-byte input and requires no authentication, but the impact is limited to a single-byte information disclosure of uninitialized heap content per invocation. There is no memory corruption, no control-flow hijack, and no denial of service. While repeated invocations could leak additional heap bytes, the standalone impact remains an info leak with no direct confidentiality breach of application-level secrets, keeping severity at LOW.
